title: Letters from Lahore
hookLine: sent away as a young man, Arjan writes longing letters to his father in verse (Majh, ang 96)

lines: HE WRITES TO HIS FATHER, IN VERSE.
cards: Have you ever written to someone you love, far away, and waited, and heard nothing back? Every few minutes, checking. Nothing.
Young Arjan is in Lahore. His father sent him there and told him to stay until he was called. So he stayed.
Weeks went by. Months. No word came.
He missed his father, who was also his teacher, his Guru. So he wrote a letter. Not in prose.

teach.h: MY MIND LONGS FOR A SIGHT OF THE GURU.
teach.b: The letter was a short hymn, now in the scripture, in raga Majh. Its first line says, in paraphrase: my mind longs for a sight of the Guru.

teach.h: LIKE THE RAINBIRD, CALLING FOR RAIN.
teach.b: It cries out like the rainbird, the chatrik, which in Indian poetry waits and calls for the one raindrop it will drink. My thirst isn't quenched, the verse says; I can't find peace without the sight of my beloved.
He sent it. No reply. He wrote a second verse, even more aching: it has been so long since he saw his beloved's face.
Still nothing. Here's what tradition says was happening.

teach.h: TWO LETTERS LOST. THE THIRD, NUMBERED.
teach.b: His eldest brother, Prithi Chand, was intercepting the letters; he didn't want Arjan anywhere near their father while the succession was open.
So when Arjan wrote a third, which says a single moment apart feels like the dark age, he marked it with a number: three. That letter reached Guru Ram Das.

The Guru saw the three, asked about the first two, found out what had happened, and sent for Arjan at once. When they met again, Arjan sang a fourth verse, the joy of reunion, and together the four make one hymn.
Sikhs call it the Shabad Hazare, and some include it in their morning prayers. Two things stand out.

teach.h: LONGING FOR A FATHER, LONGING FOR GOD.
teach.b: Longing isn't treated as weakness here: the Gurus' hymns use the language of missing someone for the soul missing God, and in this hymn, missing a father and missing God are sung as one ache.
And tradition tells the waiting as the test. Arjan never stopped writing, and he never stopped waiting.

how: The Shabad Hazare, Guru Arjan's four verses of longing from Lahore, are in the Guru Granth Sahib in raga Majh, and some Sikhs include them in their morning prayers.

o: Arjan's four verses of longing, one hymn
a long hymn of a thousand verses
letters Prithi Chand sent his father

games.q: what's inside the letters — tap the pairs.
p: the rainbird that calls for rain

s: Arjan's letters were ordinary prose notes
they were verses, and they're in the scripture, in raga Majh.
tradition says Prithi Chand intercepted the first letters
so Arjan numbered the third, and it got through.
on this path, longing is a sign of weak faith
the Gurus use longing to describe the soul missing God.

games.q: you're far from home. you've written to your father twice and heard nothing. what do you do?
o: write again, and number the letter.
games.why: tradition says Arjan marked the third letter with a number. it reached his father, who learned of the first two and called him home.

practice: Think of someone you miss: far away, out of touch, or gone. Find one line, not a whole letter, just what you'd say if they were in the room, and write it on paper or in a note on your phone. Whether you send it is up to you.

wordCard.voice: Shabad Hazare. The hymn made of young Arjan's four verses of longing to his father from Lahore, now part of some Sikhs' morning prayers.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: lochai, longs; the word in the first line, my mind longs for a sight of the Guru.

carryVoice: Your line: my mind longs. Four verses, one hymn, and the third one numbered. Day fifty-eight, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Majh, Guru Arjan, Ang 96–97 (Shabad Hazare: my mind longs for a sight of the Guru)
